title: No Top, No Bottom
hookLine: Brahma and Vishnu are arguing about which of them is greater when a pillar of fire splits the sky between them
carry: the linga: a sign of the God beyond measure
tomorrow: what happens when a father shuts Shiva out?

cards: Two gods are arguing. Brahma, the creator, says he's the greatest, since everything came from him. Vishnu, the preserver, says no, he is, since he keeps everything going.
The argument gets hot. Then, between the two of them, a pillar of fire appears, blazing, going up past where they can see and down past where they can see. No top in sight, and no bottom.
Both gods stop mid-sentence. You heard this on Shivaratri, back on day ninety; today it comes from the Shiva Purana itself.

teach.b: The Shiva Purana is a big book of Shiva's stories, told aloud by a storyteller named Suta to a gathering of sages; the path takes selections. The two gods agree on a test: whoever finds the end of this thing wins.

teach.h: A BOAR DIGS, A SWAN FLIES.
teach.b: Vishnu becomes a boar and digs down. Brahma becomes a swan and flies up. Vishnu finds no bottom, and finally comes back and says so.

But on the way he meets a ketaki flower drifting down, and he has an idea. He comes back, says he reached the top, and brings the flower along to swear it's true. Then the pillar opens and Shiva steps out of it.
He honors Vishnu for telling the truth and rebukes Brahma for the lie, and in the story the ketaki flower, the false witness, is not to be offered in Shiva's worship.

teach.h: LINGA: A SIGN OF THE UNMEASURED.
teach.b: Linga means a mark, a sign.

For Shaiva devotees, the linga in a Shiva temple recalls this pillar, and that's why the main image in so many Shiva temples has no face and no arms: it's a sign of what can't be measured, God with no top and no bottom, beyond every form.

Temple walls carve the moment, Shiva stepping out of the pillar, the boar below, the swan above; it's called Lingodbhava. And the one who comes out well is the one who admitted it: I couldn't find the end.
Before God that big, the story honors the honest answer.

how: Shaiva Hindus worship Shiva in the form of the linga in temples and homes, and the story of the endless pillar of fire is told and carved in temples as the appearance of the linga, Lingodbhava; it is also linked to Maha Shivaratri.

games.q: the pillar of fire — tap the pairs.
p: became a boar and dug down
became a swan and flew up
a sign: God with no top and no bottom

s: Brahma reached the top of the pillar
he found no top. he came back and claimed he had, with the ketaki flower as a false witness.
Vishnu admitted he couldn't find the bottom
and Shiva honored him for the truth.
in the story, the ketaki flower becomes a favorite offering to Shiva
the false witness is not to be offered in Shiva's worship.

games.q: you're Brahma. you've flown up and up and found no top. a flower drifts past. what do you do?
o: come back and admit you couldn't find it.
bring the flower back and say you reached the top.
games.why: Brahma brings the ketaki as a witness to a lie. Shiva steps out of the pillar and honors Vishnu, who told the truth.

practice: Bring to mind one big question you have no answer to and let it stand in front of you like the pillar, too big to measure. Let any quick answer drift by, like the flower.

Then do what devotees do at a Shiva temple, in your mind or with a cup of water at the sink: pour a little water, slowly, as if over the linga. If you pray, say Om Namah Shivaya, bowing to Shiva, or the name of God you use.
If you don't, let the water run and say: I don't know the end of this, and that's honest.
